claim: Interactions between excitatory and inhibitory neurons are critical to computations in cortical circuits.
source: Interactions between excitatory and inhibitory neurons are critical to computations in cortical circuits but their organization is difficult to assess with standard electrophysiological approaches.
evidence: This is a general statement about cortical circuits supported by established neuroscience knowledge.

claim: The organization of excitatory-inhibitory interactions is difficult to assess with standard electrophysiological approaches.
source: Interactions between excitatory and inhibitory neurons are critical to computations in cortical circuits but their organization is difficult to assess with standard electrophysiological approaches.
evidence: This statement reflects known limitations of standard electrophysiological methods.

claim: Within the medial entorhinal cortex, representation of location by grid and other spatial cells involves circuits in layer 2.
source: Within the medial entorhinal cortex, representation of location by grid and other spatial cells involves circuits in layer 2 in which excitatory stellate cells interact with each other via inhibitory parvalbumin expressing interneurons.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge about MEC circuits and grid cells.

claim: In layer 2 of the MEC, excitatory stellate cells interact with each other via inhibitory parvalbumin expressing interneurons.
source: Within the medial entorhinal cortex, representation of location by grid and other spatial cells involves circuits in layer 2 in which excitatory stellate cells interact with each other via inhibitory parvalbumin expressing interneurons.
evidence: This is supported by prior research on MEC connectivity.

claim: Extensive axonal projections support spatially organized connectivity between stellate cells and parvalbumin interneurons.
source: We find that extensive axonal projections support spatially organized connectivity between stellate cells and parvalbumin interneurons, such that direct connections are often, but not always, shared by nearby neurons, whereas multisynaptic interactions coordinate inputs to neurons with greater spatial separation.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on experimental data from optogenetic activation and patch-clamp recordings.

claim: Direct connections between stellate cells and parvalbumin interneurons are often, but not always, shared by nearby neurons.
source: We find that extensive axonal projections support spatially organized connectivity between stellate cells and parvalbumin interneurons, such that direct connections are often, but not always, shared by nearby neurons, whereas multisynaptic interactions coordinate inputs to neurons with greater spatial separation.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on cross-correlation analyses of synaptic responses.

claim: Multisynaptic interactions coordinate inputs to neurons with greater spatial separation.
source: We find that extensive axonal projections support spatially organized connectivity between stellate cells and parvalbumin interneurons, such that direct connections are often, but not always, shared by nearby neurons, whereas multisynaptic interactions coordinate inputs to neurons with greater spatial separation.
evidence: This is based on experimental data showing GABAzine-sensitive coordination at longer distances.

claim: Direct excitatory-inhibitory synaptic interactions may operate at the scale of grid cell clusters.
source: We suggest that direct excitatory-inhibitory synaptic interactions may operate at the scale of grid cell clusters, with local modules defined by excitatory-inhibitory connectivity, while indirect interactions may coordinate activity at the scale of grid cell modules.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Indirect interactions may coordinate activity at the scale of grid cell modules.
source: We suggest that direct excitatory-inhibitory synaptic interactions may operate at the scale of grid cell clusters, with local modules defined by excitatory-inhibitory connectivity, while indirect interactions may coordinate activity at the scale of grid cell modules.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the spatial extent of multisynaptic coordination.

claim: Simultaneous patch-clamp recordings from pairs of neurons provide a gold standard for assessment of functional properties of synaptic connections.
source: For example, while simultaneous patch-clamp recordings from pairs of neurons provide a gold standard for assessment of functional properties of synaptic connections (Markram et al., 1997; Sjöström et al., 2001), even with impressive advances in maximizing the numbers of simultaneously recorded neurons (Peng et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2015), their low throughput makes them less well suited to investigation of the spatial extent and organization of connectivity.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Paired patch-clamp recordings have low throughput, making them less well suited to investigation of the spatial extent and organization of connectivity.
source: For example, while simultaneous patch-clamp recordings from pairs of neurons provide a gold standard for assessment of functional properties of synaptic connections (Markram et al., 1997; Sjöström et al., 2001), even with impressive advances in maximizing the numbers of simultaneously recorded neurons (Peng et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2015), their low throughput makes them less well suited to investigation of the spatial extent and organization of connectivity.
evidence: This is based on known limitations of the technique and cited references.

claim: The medial entorhinal cortex is a promising higher order cortical area for elucidation of principles for circuit level computations.
source: The medial entorhinal cortex (MEC) is a promising higher order cortical area for elucidation of principles for circuit level computations (Moser and Moser, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Grid cells in the MEC have spatially periodic firing properties.
source: The striking spatially periodic firing properties of grid cells found within the MEC has an anatomical organization that shares features with the columnar organization of sensory cortices (Burgalossi and Brecht, 2014; Naumann et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge about grid cells supported by citations.

claim: The anatomical organization of grid cells shares features with the columnar organization of sensory cortices.
source: The striking spatially periodic firing properties of grid cells found within the MEC has an anatomical organization that shares features with the columnar organization of sensory cortices (Burgalossi and Brecht, 2014; Naumann et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Nearby grid cells have a similar spatial scale and orientation.
source: Nearby grid cells have a similar spatial scale and orientation, which is maintained across superficial and deep cell layers (Sargolini et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Grid cell spatial scale and orientation is maintained across superficial and deep cell layers.
source: Nearby grid cells have a similar spatial scale and orientation, which is maintained across superficial and deep cell layers (Sargolini et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: For grid cells at different dorsoventral locations the scale and orientation of their firing fields varies, with larger scales found in more ventral neurons.
source: For grid cells at different dorsoventral locations the scale and orientation of their firing fields varies, with larger scales found in more ventral neurons (Hafting et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Grid cells form discrete functional modules with similar scale and orientation.
source: This variability arises from discrete groups of grid cells that have firing fields with similar scale and orientation and form functional modules (Barry et al., 2007; Gu et al., 2018; Stensola et al., 2012; Yoon et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Individual grid cell modules can be partitioned into cell clusters, with each cluster containing topographically ordered grid cells encoding the full range of possible spatial phases.
source: Individual modules can be partitioned into cell clusters, with each cluster containing topographically ordered grid cells encoding the full range of possible spatial phases (Gu et al., 2018; Heys et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Synaptic interactions between excitatory stellate cells and inhibitory parvalbumin positive interneurons in layer 2 of the MEC have received attention as a possible substrate for emergence of grid firing fields.
source: Within layer 2 of the MEC, synaptic interactions between excitatory stellate cells (SCs) and inhibitory parvalbumin positive interneurons (PV+ INs) have received attention as a possible substrate for emergence of grid firing fields (Beed et al., 2013; Buetfering et al., 2014; Couey et al., 2013; Miao et al., 2017; Pastoll et al., 2013; Shipston-Sharman et al., 2016; Widloski and Fiete, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Layer 2 of the MEC contains a high density of grid cells.
source: Layer 2 of the MEC contains a high density of grid cells, with both stellate and pyramidal cells (PCs) in this layer having grid fields (Domnisoru et al., 2013; Gu et al., 2018; Heys et al., 2014; Rowland et al., 2018; Schmidt-Hieber and Häusser, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Both stellate and pyramidal cells in layer 2 of the MEC have grid fields.
source: Layer 2 of the MEC contains a high density of grid cells, with both stellate and pyramidal cells (PCs) in this layer having grid fields (Domnisoru et al., 2013; Gu et al., 2018; Heys et al., 2014; Rowland et al., 2018; Schmidt-Hieber and Häusser, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Interactions between stellate cells appear to be primarily via PV+ interneurons.
source: Interactions between SCs appear to be primarily via PV+ INs (Couey et al., 2013; Fuchs et al., 2016; Pastoll et al., 2013; Winterer et al., 2017), and models based on this connectivity are able to account for grid firing and local theta-nested gamma frequency network activity (Pastoll et al., 2013; Shipston-Sharman et al., 2016; Solanka et al., 2015; Widloski and Fiete, 2014), while silencing PV+ INs reduces the spatial periodicity of grid firing in layer 2 (Miao et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Models based on SC-PV+ IN connectivity are able to account for grid firing and local theta-nested gamma frequency network activity.
source: Interactions between SCs appear to be primarily via PV+ INs (Couey et al., 2013; Fuchs et al., 2016; Pastoll et al., 2013; Winterer et al., 2017), and models based on this connectivity are able to account for grid firing and local theta-nested gamma frequency network activity (Pastoll et al., 2013; Shipston-Sharman et al., 2016; Solanka et al., 2015; Widloski and Fiete, 2014), while silencing PV+ INs reduces the spatial periodicity of grid firing in layer 2 (Miao et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior modeling work.

claim: Silencing PV+ interneurons reduces the spatial periodicity of grid firing in layer 2.
source: Interactions between SCs appear to be primarily via PV+ INs (Couey et al., 2013; Fuchs et al., 2016; Pastoll et al., 2013; Winterer et al., 2017), and models based on this connectivity are able to account for grid firing and local theta-nested gamma frequency network activity (Pastoll et al., 2013; Shipston-Sharman et al., 2016; Solanka et al., 2015; Widloski and Fiete, 2014), while silencing PV+ INs reduces the spatial periodicity of grid firing in layer 2 (Miao et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior experimental work.

claim: Previous investigations of interactions between stellate cells and PV+ interneurons have focused on nearby pairs of cells, typically separated by <150 µm.
source: However, previous investigation of interactions between SCs and PV+ INs have focused on nearby pairs of cells, typically separated by <150 µm (Couey et al., 2013; Dhillon and Jones, 2000; Fernandez et al., 2022; Fuchs et al., 2016; Grosser et al., 2021; Pastoll et al., 2013; Winterer et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Stellate cells have axon collaterals in deep L1, L2, L3 close to the border with L4, and in L5b.
source: Consistent with observations from labeling of presynaptic terminals (Sürmeli et al., 2015), we found axon collaterals of SCs in deep L1, L2, L3 close to the border with L4, and in L5b (Figure 1A–E).
evidence: This is based on experimental data from neuronal reconstructions and is consistent with prior work.

claim: The dendrites of stellate cells were exclusively in L1-2 and the superficial part of L3.
source: The dendrites of SCs were exclusively in L1-2 and the superficial part of L3.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from neuronal reconstructions.

claim: Individual stellate cells varied in whether they had axon collaterals in a particular layer.
source: Individual SCs varied in whether they had axon collaterals in a particular layer (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is based on experimental data from neuronal reconstructions.

claim: The total length of axon collaterals in superficial layers (L1-3) was greater than in deep layers (L5-6).
source: While the total length of axon collaterals in superficial layers (L1-3) was greater than in deep layers (L5-6), there was no apparent relationship between the total length of superficial and deep axon collaterals (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is based on experimental data from neuronal reconstructions.

claim: There was no apparent relationship between the total length of superficial and deep axon collaterals in stellate cells.
source: While the total length of axon collaterals in superficial layers (L1-3) was greater than in deep layers (L5-6), there was no apparent relationship between the total length of superficial and deep axon collaterals (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of experimental data (linear model: p=0.30).

claim: For stellate cells with axon collaterals in L1-3, the average extent of their collaterals was >500 µm along the dorsoventral axis in sagittal slices.
source: For SCs with axon collaterals in L1-3, the average extent of their collaterals was >500 µm along the dorsoventral axis in sagittal slices, and >400 µm along the mediolateral axis in horizontal slices (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is based on experimental data from neuronal reconstructions.

claim: For stellate cells with axon collaterals in L1-3, the average extent of their collaterals was >400 µm along the mediolateral axis in horizontal slices.
source: For SCs with axon collaterals in L1-3, the average extent of their collaterals was >500 µm along the dorsoventral axis in sagittal slices, and >400 µm along the mediolateral axis in horizontal slices (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is based on experimental data from neuronal reconstructions.

claim: Ramp-like increases in the intensity of wide field illumination drive asynchronous action potential firing by stellate cells expressing channelrhodopsin-2.
source: As a first approach, we used ramp-like increases in the intensity of wide field illumination to drive asynchronous action potential firing by SCs expressing channelrhodopsin-2 (ChR2) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on experimental data showing variable spike timing across trials.

claim: The timing of action potentials fired by stellate cells activated with ramp illumination differs across trials and between activated cells.
source: As the timing of action potentials fired by SCs activated in this way differs across trials and between activated cells (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1), we reasoned that temporally correlated synaptic inputs to postsynaptic PV+ INs would indicate coordinated input from the activated SCs.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from simultaneous recordings of ChR2-expressing stellate cells.

claim: Activation of stellate cells with light ramps induced excitatory postsynaptic currents in all PV+ interneurons.
source: Activation of SCs with light ramps induced excitatory postsynaptic currents (EPSCs) in all PV+ INs (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: This is based on experimental data from voltage-clamp recordings.

claim: 35 out of 71 recorded pairs of PV+ interneurons were identified as receiving coordinated synaptic input from stellate cells.
source: In this way, we identified 35/71 recorded pairs as receiving coordinated synaptic input from SCs (yellow points in Figure 3E–F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D), but 0/1000 shuffled pairs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of cross-correlation data compared to shuffled controls.

claim: Pairs of PV+ interneurons that received coordinated synaptic input from stellate cells were separated by distances up to 500 µm along the dorsoventral axis.
source: Pairs of PV+ INs that received coordinated synaptic input from SCs were separated by distances up to 500 µm along the dorsoventral axis and up to 900 µm along the mediolateral axis (Figure 3E–F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-B).
evidence: This is based on experimental data from simultaneous recordings at various distances.

claim: Pairs of PV+ interneurons that received coordinated synaptic input from stellate cells were separated by distances up to 900 µm along the mediolateral axis.
source: Pairs of PV+ INs that received coordinated synaptic input from SCs were separated by distances up to 500 µm along the dorsoventral axis and up to 900 µm along the mediolateral axis (Figure 3E–F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-B).
evidence: This is based on experimental data from simultaneous recordings at various distances.

claim: Peak cross-correlation coefficients between PV+ interneurons were correlated with intercell distance along the dorsoventral axis.
source: Peak cross-correlation coefficients were correlated with intercell distance along the dorsoventral (adjusted R2=0.19, p=0.0046, F1,34 = 9.2) and mediolateral axes (adjusted R2=0.09, p=0.045, F1,33 = 4.3), whereas variance of the lags did not show a detectable dependence on distance (horizontal: adjusted R2=0.006, p=0.27, F1,34 = 1.2; vertical: adjusted R2=–0.03, p=1.0, F1,33 = 0.0).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Peak cross-correlation coefficients between PV+ interneurons were correlated with intercell distance along the mediolateral axis.
source: Peak cross-correlation coefficients were correlated with intercell distance along the dorsoventral (adjusted R2=0.19, p=0.0046, F1,34 = 9.2) and mediolateral axes (adjusted R2=0.09, p=0.045, F1,33 = 4.3), whereas variance of the lags did not show a detectable dependence on distance (horizontal: adjusted R2=0.006, p=0.27, F1,34 = 1.2; vertical: adjusted R2=–0.03, p=1.0, F1,33 = 0.0).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: 3 of 49 pairs of tested PV+ interneurons were electrically coupled to one another.
source: We found that 3 of 49 pairs of tested PV+ INs were electrically coupled to one another (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on experimental data from paired recordings testing electrical coupling.

claim: All three electrically coupled pairs of PV+ interneurons were separated by distances <100 µm.
source: All three electrically coupled pairs were separated by distances <100 µm and received coordinated synaptic input during optogenetic activation of SCs.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from paired recordings.

claim: No evidence was found for inhibitory connectivity between 49 tested pairs of PV+ interneurons.
source: We did not find any evidence for inhibitory connectivity between 49 tested pairs of PV+ INs.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from paired recordings testing chemical synaptic connections.

claim: For pairs of PV+ interneurons separated by <150 µm, blocking GABAA receptors did not affect their coordinated responses to ramp activation of stellate cells.
source: We found that for pairs of PV+ INs that received coordinated input in control conditions and were separated by <150 µm, when GABAA receptors were blocked their responses to ramp activation of SCs were similar (Figure 4A–B and D–E).
evidence: This is based on experimental data comparing responses before and after GABAzine application.

claim: For PV+ interneurons separated by >150 µm, blocking GABAA receptors typically reduced peak cross-correlation coefficients and increased cross-correlation lag variance.
source: By contrast, for PV+ INs separated by >150 µm, CC_peak_mean was typically reduced and CC_lag_var increased, and in many cases responses to ramp activation of SCs were no longer consistent with the PV+ INs receiving coordinated inputs (Figure 4C–E), indicating that in control conditions their shared input resulted from recruitment of inhibitory neurons.
evidence: This is based on experimental data comparing responses before and after GABAzine application.

claim: Focal laser stimulation of ChR2 expressing stellate cells asynchronously activates restricted populations of cells.
source: We reasoned that if focal light pulses asynchronously activate restricted populations of ChR2 expressing SCs, then simultaneous postsynaptic responses in pairs of PV+ INs will identify inputs from the same SC.
evidence: This is based on experimental validation showing variable spike latencies with focal stimulation.

claim: At threshold stimulation intensities, the timing of action potentials in stellate cells was variable between trials.
source: At threshold stimulation intensities the timing of action potentials was variable between trials (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C) and action potentials were typically triggered from a single location (1.63±0.74 locations, proportion of responses 0.53±0.36; n=8 cells, N=4 mice, Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is based on experimental data from recordings of ChR2-expressing stellate cells.

claim: At threshold stimulation intensities, action potentials in stellate cells were typically triggered from a single location.
source: At threshold stimulation intensities the timing of action potentials was variable between trials (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C) and action potentials were typically triggered from a single location (1.63±0.74 locations, proportion of responses 0.53±0.36; n=8 cells, N=4 mice, Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is based on experimental data from recordings of ChR2-expressing stellate cells.

claim: High correlation probabilities indicative of common synaptic input were found only for PV+ interneurons within 200 µm in sagittal slices.
source: When we investigated the variation in the correlation probability as a function of separation between PV+ INs, we found high correlation probabilities indicative of common synaptic input only for PV+ INs within 200 µm in sagittal slices and within 400 µm in horizontal slices (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is based on experimental data from focal stimulation experiments.

claim: High correlation probabilities indicative of common synaptic input were found only for PV+ interneurons within 400 µm in horizontal slices.
source: When we investigated the variation in the correlation probability as a function of separation between PV+ INs, we found high correlation probabilities indicative of common synaptic input only for PV+ INs within 200 µm in sagittal slices and within 400 µm in horizontal slices (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is based on experimental data from focal stimulation experiments.

claim: The correlation probability was independent of the number of activated stellate cells.
source: We found that the correlation probability was independent of the number of activated SCs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1H), suggesting that differential sampling of SC axons does not account for the variation in correlation probability between nearby pairs of PV+ INs.
evidence: This is based on experimental data comparing correlation probabilities at different stimulus intensities.

claim: Most cross-correlation scores between stimulus maps of simultaneously recorded PV+ interneurons differed significantly from chance.
source: We found that most cross-correlation scores differed significantly from chance, and maps could be positively or negatively correlated (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of experimental data to shuffled controls.

claim: Stimulus maps of PV+ interneuron pairs could be positively or negatively correlated.
source: We found that most cross-correlation scores differed significantly from chance, and maps could be positively or negatively correlated (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is based on experimental data from focal stimulation experiments.

claim: Almost all PV+ interneurons had dense axonal arborizations within layer 2.
source: In contrast to the relatively sparse axon collaterals of SCs, almost all PV+ INs had dense axonal arborizations within layer 2 and dendrites primarily within layers 1 and 2 (Figure 6A–F).
evidence: This is based on experimental data from neuronal reconstructions.

claim: PV+ interneurons had dendrites primarily within layers 1 and 2.
source: In contrast to the relatively sparse axon collaterals of SCs, almost all PV+ INs had dense axonal arborizations within layer 2 and dendrites primarily within layers 1 and 2 (Figure 6A–F).
evidence: This is based on experimental data from neuronal reconstructions.

claim: Axonal projections to deep layers of the MEC were not observed in PV+ interneurons.
source: We did not observe axonal projections to deep layers of the MEC.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from neuronal reconstructions.

claim: The maximal dorsoventral and mediolateral extent of the axons of PV+ interneurons was on average >600 µm.
source: The maximal dorsoventral and mediolateral extent of the axons of these neurons was on average >600 µm, and in both orientations was greater than the corresponding extent of their dendrites (sagittal p=3.15 x 10–6 n=17, Horizontal p=8.9 x 10–4 n=7; Figure 6G).
evidence: This is based on experimental data from neuronal reconstructions.

claim: The maximal extent of PV+ interneuron axons was greater than that of their dendrites in both dorsoventral and mediolateral orientations.
source: The maximal dorsoventral and mediolateral extent of the axons of these neurons was on average >600 µm, and in both orientations was greater than the corresponding extent of their dendrites (sagittal p=3.15 x 10–6 n=17, Horizontal p=8.9 x 10–4 n=7; Figure 6G).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of experimental data from neuronal reconstructions.

claim: Activation of PV+ interneurons with ramp stimuli induced inhibitory synaptic responses in stellate cells.
source: When populations of PV+ INs were asynchronously activated using ramp stimuli, recordings from SCs revealed inhibitory synaptic responses.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from voltage-clamp recordings.

claim: PV+ interneuron-driven synaptic currents recorded from stellate cells were relatively sparse and often of large amplitude.
source: In contrast to the responses of PV+ INs to activation of SCs, PV+ IN-driven synaptic currents recorded from SCs were relatively sparse and often of large amplitude (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is based on experimental data from voltage-clamp recordings.

claim: The cell bodies of pairs of stellate cells receiving common input from PV+ interneurons were separated by <300 µm along dorsoventral and mediolateral axes.
source: The cell bodies of pairs receiving common input were separated by <300 µm along dorsoventral and mediolateral axes (Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is based on experimental data from simultaneous recordings.

claim: No pairs of stellate cells and pyramidal cells were found with correlated responses suggesting a common input from PV+ interneurons.
source: We did not find any pairs of SCs and pyramidal cells with correlated responses that suggested a common input (Figure 7E and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C and F), indicating that they receive input from distinct populations of PV+ INs.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from simultaneous recordings of SC-pyramidal cell pairs.

claim: Stellate cells and pyramidal cells receive input from distinct populations of PV+ interneurons.
source: We did not find any pairs of SCs and pyramidal cells with correlated responses that suggested a common input (Figure 7E and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C and F), indicating that they receive input from distinct populations of PV+ INs.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental finding that no SC-pyramidal cell pairs showed correlated responses.

claim: Direct functional interactions between stellate cells and PV+ interneurons in L2 of the MEC appear localized largely to within ~250 µm.
source: Using these approaches, we find that direct functional interactions between SCs and PV+ INs in L2 of the MEC appear localized largely to within ~250 µm.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings from multiple approaches.

claim: The probability of shared connectivity between stellate cells and PV+ interneurons is variable.
source: The probability of shared connectivity in each direction is variable, with functional connections from SCs to PV+ INs appearing to be demarcated by distinct boundaries.
evidence: This is based on experimental data showing variable correlation probabilities and spatial organization.

claim: Functional connections from stellate cells to PV+ interneurons appear to be demarcated by distinct boundaries.
source: The probability of shared connectivity in each direction is variable, with functional connections from SCs to PV+ INs appearing to be demarcated by distinct boundaries.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from focal stimulation showing clear borders in stimulus maps.

claim: PV+ interneurons separated by <100 µm interact through gap junction connections.
source: First, PV+ INs separated by <100 µm interact through gap junction connections (see also Fernandez et al., 2022).
evidence: This is based on experimental data showing electrical coupling and is supported by a citation.

claim: Populations of interacting PV+ interneurons and stellate cells separated by up to ~250 µm form local modules defined by common inputs.
source: Second, populations of interacting PV+ INs and SCs separated by up to ~250 µm form local modules defined by the common inputs between each cell population (see also Couey et al., 2013; Dhillon and Jones, 2000; Fuchs et al., 2016; Pastoll et al., 2013; Winterer et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on experimental data and is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Longer range output from stellate cells to non-PV interneurons may support coordination between modules.
source: Third, longer range output from SCs to non-PV INs may support coordination between modules.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the experimental findings of indirect coordination.

claim: Interneurons in L1 of the MEC could be candidates for coordination between modules.
source: Candidates for this coordination could include interneurons in L1 of the MEC (Vandrey et al., 2022), which can have extensive intra-laminar axons (Shi et al., 2023), or somatostatin-positive interneurons in layer 2 (Fernandez et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a speculative suggestion supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Somatostatin-positive interneurons in layer 2 could be candidates for coordination between modules.
source: Candidates for this coordination could include interneurons in L1 of the MEC (Vandrey et al., 2022), which can have extensive intra-laminar axons (Shi et al., 2023), or somatostatin-positive interneurons in layer 2 (Fernandez et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a speculative suggestion supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Local shared inputs from stellate cells to PV+ interneurons could form a substrate for computation within grid cell clusters.
source: In principle, local shared inputs from SCs to PV+ INs, and vice versa, could form a substrate for computation within grid cell clusters.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Connectivity between stellate cells and PV+ interneurons could support emergence of activity bumps through excitatory-inhibitory interactions.
source: Given the continuous attractor dynamics of grid cell populations observed experimentally (Barry et al., 2007; Gardner et al., 2021; Yoon et al., 2013), such connectivity could support emergence of activity bumps through excitatory-inhibitory interactions (Guanella et al., 2007; Pastoll et al., 2013; Shipston-Sharman et al., 2016; Widloski et al., 2018; Widloski and Fiete, 2014).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations to prior experimental and modeling work.

claim: The incomplete connectivity between local stellate cells and PV+ interneurons is consistent with structured connections expected within networks with continuous attractor dynamics.
source: The incomplete connectivity between local SCs and PV+ INs is consistent with structured connections expected within networks with continuous attractor dynamics (Pastoll et al., 2013; Shipston-Sharman et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings supported by citations to prior modeling work.
